the dispersal of matter and Entropy (S) is a measure of the disorder in a system. The more predictable the 
energy ina system. states of individual particles (atoms, molecules or ions) in a system are, the 
lower the entropy of that system, and vice versa. 
In a solid lattice, all particles have fixed positions, and their movement is 
limited to vibration and rotation, so entropy values of solid substances are 
low. Liquids have higher entropies than solids because their particles have no 
fixed coordinates, and they can move in random directions with respect to 
one another. However, the particles of a liquid interact with one another, and 
the distances between adjacent particles vary only slightly, so the difference 
in entropy between solid and liquid states of the same substance is relatively 
small. In contrast, gases have very high entropy values because their particles 
move freely, the intermolecular distances vary over greater ranges, and both 
the positions and kinetic energies of individual particles are completely 
unpredictable. Therefore, for the same substance, the entropy values increase 
from solid to liquid and from liquid to gaseous state (figure 9).

When [reactants] >> [products], the forward reaction is favoured because 
its Gibbs energy change (AG, in figure 10) is negative. Therefore, reactants 
spontaneously transform into products until the state of equilibrium is reached. 
At equilibrium, AG =0, so neither the forward nor the reverse reaction is 
favoured. The reaction mixture can remain in this state indefinitely unless the 
equilibrium is disturbed by external factors. 
When [reactants] << [products], the forward reaction becomes non￾spontaneous because its Gibbs energy change (AG, in figure 10) is positive. In 
contrast, the reverse reaction becomes spontaneous because its Gibbs energy 
change has the same magnitude as AG, but the opposite sign. Therefore, 
products spontaneously transform into reactants until the state of equilibrium 
is reached. 
The actual AG value for any given composition of the reaction mixture can be 
calculated using the following expression: 
AG=AG® +RTInQ 
where AG® is the standard Gibbs energy change for the reaction, 
R =8.31)K " mol™is the gas constant, T is the absolute temperature (in kelvin), 
and Q is the reaction quotient, which represents relative concentrations of

If a liquid does not freeze or boil spontaneously under certain conditions (T0 and p0), then the ΔG values for both freezing and boiling of that liquid at T0 are positive. Boiling is endothermic (ΔHb > 0), and the entropy change of boiling is positive (ΔSb > 0). According to the Gibbs equation, if ΔGb > 0, then ΔHb > T0 ΔSb. The boiling will become spontaneous only when T0ΔSb increases, which can only happen when the temperature increases (Tb > T0). Freezing is exothermic (ΔHf < 0), and the entropy change of freezing is negative (ΔSf < 0). According to the Gibbs equation, if ΔGf > 0, then ΔHf > T0ΔSf. The freezing will become spontaneous only when T0ΔSf increases (becomes less negative), which can only happen when the temperature decreases (Tf < T0).
Therefore, if Tb > T0 and Tf < T0, then Tb > Tf.
